title: Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl
author: Anne Frank
short_summary: Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who, with her family, went into hiding in Amsterdam in 1942 to escape Nazi persecution during World War II. For over two years she kept a diary - addressed to an imaginary friend she called 'Kitty' - recording daily life in the cramped hiding place, her hopes, fears, and growth as a young writer. The diary ends shortly before the hiding place was discovered; of the eight people who hid there, only Anne's father survived.
extended_summary:
Anne Frank was given a diary for her thirteenth birthday, on 12 June 1942. Three weeks later her older sister Margot received a call-up notice from the Nazi authorities, and the family went into hiding the next day in rooms behind Otto Frank's business premises on the Prinsengracht in Amsterdam. The entrance was concealed behind a movable bookcase. Four more people joined them: Hermann, Auguste and Peter van Pels, and later Fritz Pfeffer, who shared Anne's small room. In the diary Anne gave them other names — the van Daans, and Albert Dussel.

For more than two years they never went outside. During office hours they could not run water, use the toilet or speak above a whisper, because the workers below must not hear them; in the evenings and at weekends they could move about, listen to the radio and study. Anne wrote to 'Kitty' about all of it: the boredom and the fear, burglaries in the building at night, quarrels over food and space, her difficult relationship with her mother, her closeness to her father, her growing friendship with Peter, and her determination to become a writer. In March 1944 a Dutch minister broadcasting from London asked people to keep their diaries and letters as a record of the occupation, and Anne began rewriting hers for publication.

Her last entry is dated 1 August 1944. Three days later the hiding place was discovered and everyone in it was arrested and deported. Anne died at Bergen-Belsen early in 1945. Of the eight, only her father Otto survived; Miep Gies, one of the helpers, had gathered up the scattered papers and kept them safe, and gave them to him after the war.

questions.prompt: The family went into hiding sooner than planned because one of them received a call-up notice from the Nazi authorities. Who received it?

options: Margot, Anne's sister
Otto, Anne's father
Edith, Anne's mother
Anne, the diary's writer

questions.explanation: The notice was for Margot, and it arrived on 5 July 1942; the family went into hiding the very next morning. Anne records her own shock at learning it was her sister who had been called, not her father as she had first assumed — one of the moments where the diary corrects what a reader might expect.

questions.prompt: Anne addressed her entries to "Kitty", a person who did not exist. Why did she write to an imaginary friend rather than simply keeping a journal?

options: She wanted the diary to be the close friend she felt she lacked
She was told that a diary should always be written as letters
She hoped a friend of that name would one day read the book
She wanted to hide who she was in case the diary was found

questions.explanation: Anne writes that she has plenty of acquaintances but no one she can tell everything to — so the paper itself has to be that person. It also shapes the whole book: because she is writing to someone, she explains, argues and confides rather than just listing events.

questions.prompt: The doorway to the hiding place was hidden from anyone walking past by a movable ___.
questions.explanation: It was built by Johan Voskuijl, the father of Bep, one of the helpers. A hinged bookcase in a working office building is an ordinary object that hides a doorway completely — and it is the reason the group stayed undiscovered for more than two years.

questions.prompt: In the diary, the other family sharing the hiding place is never called by its real name. What name does Anne give them?

options: The van Daans
The Voskuijls
The Kleimans
The Pfeffers

questions.explanation: Hermann, Auguste and Peter van Pels appear as the van Daan family, and Fritz Pfeffer appears as Albert Dussel. Anne invented the names herself when she began rewriting the diary for publication — she was already thinking like an author protecting the people in her book.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Anne's diary and her life in the order they happened.

items: Anne is given a diary for her thirteenth birthday
A call-up notice arrives for Margot from the authorities
The families move into the rooms behind the bookcase
A radio broadcast asks Dutch people to keep their diaries
Anne writes the last entry in her diary
The hiding place is discovered and everyone is arrested

questions.explanation: Only three weeks separate the birthday present from the day the family disappeared from view. The broadcast in March 1944 falls near the end, which matters: for the last months Anne was not only keeping a diary, she was rewriting it as a book she hoped strangers would read.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their part in the story the diary tells.

right: A helper who brought food and news, and later saved the papers
The eighth person, who shared Anne's small room
The boy in hiding whom Anne grows close to during 1944
The parent Anne felt understood her best

questions.explanation: The diary is as much about these four relationships as about the war. Anne is grateful to the helpers, irritated by having to share a room with a grown man she barely knew, uncertain and then hopeful about Peter, and closer to her father than to anyone else in the building.

questions.prompt: Life in the hiding place ran on a strict timetable. Sort each of these by when it was possible.

content.groupA: Only during office hours, when the workers were below
content.groupB: Only in the evenings, at night or at weekends

options.label: Speaking in whispers and walking in stockinged feet
Leaving the tap unused and the toilet unflushed
Sitting perfectly still for hours at a stretch
Moving freely between the rooms of the Annex
Listening to the radio down in the private office
Washing, cooking and talking in a normal voice

questions.explanation: This timetable is what makes the diary so different from a history book. The danger was not usually dramatic — it was the daily discipline of being silent from morning until six o'clock, every weekday, for over two years, in rooms just above people who had no idea they were there.

questions.prompt: In March 1944 the group heard a Dutch minister broadcasting from London, asking people to keep diaries and letters as a record of the occupation. What did Anne do about it?

options: She began rewriting her diary as a book for others to read
She stopped writing, in case the diary was used against them
She started a second diary about the news from the radio
She asked the helpers to take her pages out of the building

questions.explanation: Anne went back to the beginning and rewrote entries, cutting, sharpening and inventing names for everyone, with a title already in mind. It changes how we read the later diary: she is no longer only confiding in Kitty, she is working as a writer who expects an audience.

questions.prompt: Not long before the arrest, Anne wrote that in spite of everything she still believed people were really good at heart. Knowing what was happening outside, and what happened to her afterwards, what do you make of that sentence? Do you think it was true, or brave, or something else?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer and the question should be treated gently. A strong answer engages with the tension the child has noticed: she wrote it while being hunted, and the people who fed her were risking their lives, so the sentence can be read as evidence, as hope, or as a fifteen-year-old refusing to let cruelty have the last word. Accept agreement, disagreement or uncertainty, as long as the answer gives a reason.

questions.prompt: The people in the Annex could not go outside at all for more than two years. Write two or three sentences to Kitty, as if you were living there, about one ordinary everyday thing you would miss most — and what you would do instead.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names one specific ordinary thing — a bicycle, a street, a shop, running to school, being loud — rather than a general statement, and adds what the writer would do instead inside four walls. Accept any answer written seriously in the diary's voice.

questions.prompt: Anne wrote again and again about what she wanted to be one day. More than anything, she wanted to become a ___.
questions.explanation: She wanted to be a journalist and then a writer, and she says plainly that she wants to go on living even after her death. It is the ambition of the book: the diary was not only a refuge from the days in hiding, it was her training.

questions.prompt: How did Anne's diary survive after the arrest, so that it could be read?

options: A helper gathered the scattered pages and kept them safe
It was found in the building many years after the war
Anne posted the pages out of the building to a friend
Her father carried the pages with him when he was taken

questions.explanation: Miep Gies picked the papers up off the floor of the ransacked Annex and put them away unread, intending to return them to Anne. When Otto Frank — the only one of the eight to survive — came back, she gave them to him instead.
